Fixed admissibility constraints define a feasible assignment set F(h), but do not define probabilities over it. Minimum-cost matching selects an optimizer a*(h); deterministic tie-breaking concentrates the intervention distribution on that assignment. Random feasible sampling instead estimates sensitivity averaged over its sampling law q(a|h). Thus S(q)=E_h E_q[Δf(h,a)] generally differs between methods, even with identical constraints. This is an application of the [stochastic-intervention framework](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4117410/): optimization measures response to cost-minimizing replacements, whereas sampling measures response to distributed admissible replacements. Neither automatically measures real-world causal effects.

“Random feasible” does not imply uniform: greedy randomized construction, random edge costs followed by optimization, and uniform sampling of complete matchings generally induce different laws. [Jerrum–Sinclair–Vigoda](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~sinclair/perm2.pdf) explicitly address approximately uniform perfect-matching sampling. For reproducible comparisons, specify the target law, tie-breaking, rejection/retry rules and approximation error. Minimum cost can reduce intervention distance, but smaller distance does not guarantee smaller model response.

Recommended diagnostic design: freeze histories, replacement positions, candidate pools, admissibility edges and replacement counts; establish feasibility independently of assignment selection. Report completion rates and sensitivity separately. Compare selectors on the same feasible histories, then repeat within prespecified replacement-distance bands, checking position-specific distances and candidate characteristics. A feasibility-only matching solver provides a useful control against greedy construction failures. Report recovered histories separately; including them changes the evaluated population. Repeated assignments per history separate assignment variability from between-history variability. Importance weighting requires known probabilities and support coverage; deterministic optimizer outputs cannot recover an unrestricted random-assignment average. These recommendations follow the principle that analysis must reflect the actual [restricted assignment mechanism](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6140533/).
